reason: Acted for paid family leave.
expectedDescription: Sponsored HB 2598, a measure enacting the Kansas Paid Family Leave Act; it died in committee on 2026-04-10.

reason: Acted for support for striking teachers.
expectedDescription: As a West Virginia state senator, campaigned in support of the 2018 teachers' strike, traveling the state to speak at rallies for striking teachers.

reason: Acted for leading workers through a strike.
expectedDescription: Led the union local at Kellogg's Omaha cereal plant through the 2021 strike. As president of Local 50G of the Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers union he spoke for the strikers while talks with the company were at a standstill, saying: "We just want to go to work. That's why we're out here."

reason: Acted against voter-passed paid sick leave.
expectedDescription: Voted yes as Speaker on 2025-03-13 on third reading and passage of HCS#2 HBs 567, 546, 758 & 958, which repealed the voter-approved statewide paid sick leave requirement; the bill passed 96-51.

reason: Acted against the minimum wage for full-time students.
expectedDescription: Payne voted to allow employers to pay full-time students less than the minimum wage.

reason: Acted for stronger sick time and minimum wage rules.
expectedDescription: Said the final earned sick time and minimum wage deal fell short for workers living paycheck to paycheck. She had offered two floor amendments that day and both failed.

reason: Acted for reinstating workers fired for striking.
expectedDescription: Called on Ciena Healthcare, one of Michigan's largest nursing home operators, to reinstate workers who say they were fired for joining a one-day strike.

reason: Acted against paid parental leave for state workers.
expectedDescription: Vetoed a bill at the end of the 2026 Nebraska session that would have given all state employees six weeks of paid leave after giving birth or adopting a child. He argued the benefit already covers rules-covered public servants and union members.

reason: Acted for workers' compensation for infectious disease.
expectedDescription: Introduced Michigan House Bill 5180 of 2025, creating an infectious-disease workers' compensation presumption for essential employees during declared emergencies.

reason: Acted for prevailing wage.
expectedDescription: Voted to bring back the prevailing wage rule, which sets union-scale pay on state construction contracts. The House passed the bill 56-53.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted to repeal Michigan's right-to-work law and restore union security agreements for private sector workers. The House passed Senate Bill 34 by 56-52.

reason: Acted for a $15 minimum wage.
expectedDescription: Signed the Lifting Up Illinois Working Families Act, which raised the state minimum wage in steps to $15 an hour by 2025.

reason: Acted for earned sick leave and wage theft protections.
expectedDescription: Puja supported earned sick leave, wage-theft protections, the Immigration Protection Act, and displaced-worker protections through county committee work.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Puri voted to repeal Michigan's right-to-work law for public workers. The repeal passed 56-53.

reason: Acted for recovering unpaid wages.
expectedDescription: Raoul recovered unpaid wages for temporary workers who had been misclassified.

reason: Acted for higher workers' compensation for single parents.
expectedDescription: Sponsored a law raising workers' compensation payments for injured single parents, matching the rates paid to married workers with children. It passed the House 78-18 and the Senate 36-12 (House Bill 1788, Chapter 168, Laws of 2025).

reason: Acted for prevailing wage.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on a city law setting prevailing wages on large Phoenix construction jobs (Ordinance G-7217). The rule covers city projects costing $4 million or more. Staff estimated about $17 million a year in added capital costs. The council passed it 6-3.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on House Roll Call 20, passing 2023 House Bill 4004 by 56-53; the bill restored the ability of public-sector bargaining agreements to require agency fees from nonunion members, repealing Michigan's public-sector right-to-work law.

reason: Acted against prevailing wage.
expectedDescription: Roth voted no on House Bill 4007, which reenacted Michigan's prevailing wage requirement for state-financed construction projects; House Roll Call 22 passed the bill 56-53 along party lines and it became Public Act 10 of 2023.

reason: Acted against repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Roth voted no on House Bill 4004, the repeal of Michigan's right-to-work law for public-sector employees, which restored the ability of collective bargaining agreements to require agency fees from nonunion members; House Roll Call 20 passed the bill 56-53 with every Republican voting no.

reason: Acted against paid sick leave at smaller employers.
expectedDescription: Introduced a bill limiting Alaska's paid sick leave requirement to employers with 50 or more workers, ending it for smaller businesses (House Bill 161).

reason: Acted for paid sick leave for immigration hearings.
expectedDescription: Prime-sponsored HB 1875, allowing workers to use paid sick leave to prepare for or attend immigration proceedings, enacted as Chapter 170, 2025 Laws.

reason: Acted for a $15 minimum wage.
expectedDescription: Submitted a CBS Minnesota questionnaire response supporting a $15 statewide minimum wage and state assistance to help businesses cover it.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on House Bill 4004 (House Roll Call 20), which passed 56-53 and became Public Act 9 of 2023, restoring the ability of public-sector collective bargaining agreements to require agency fees from nonunion members and repealing Michigan's public-sector right-to-work law.

reason: Acted for workers' compensation notice.
expectedDescription: Sponsored a law requiring injured workers or their legal guardians to be told about workers' compensation and state indemnification benefits, and reopening the application window for officers with brain injuries (House Bill 1128, Act 415).

reason: Acted for prevailing wages.
expectedDescription: Sears cosponsored SB 1721, requiring prevailing wages and fringe benefits on state-sponsored or state-financed public construction contracts.

reason: Acted for prevailing wage on energy projects.
expectedDescription: Voted to require prevailing wages on large solar and wind projects that get state support. The Senate passed it 20-18.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted for repealing Michigan's right-to-work law for public employees. The repeal let union security fees return to contracts. The Senate passed it 20-17.

reason: Acted for a living minimum wage.
expectedDescription: In a published candidate questionnaire, Slade publicly advocated a living minimum wage, the Texas Dream Act, municipal authority to regulate firearms, and universally affordable childcare.

reason: Acted for equal pay and anti-retaliation protections.
expectedDescription: Authored Senate Bill 497, the Equal Pay and Anti-Retaliation Act, enacted as Chapter 612 of the 2023 statutes. It strengthened Labor Code protections against wage discrimination and retaliation. The law then presumed retaliation if an employer punished a worker within 90 days of a protected complaint. The employer could rebut that presumption.

reason: Acted against repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Smit voted against repealing Michigan's right-to-work law for public workers. The repeal passed 56-53 and let unions again charge fees to non-members.

reason: Acted for backing a student workers' strike.
expectedDescription: Backed the University of Oregon student workers' strike as president of SEIU 503 sublocal 085. She said her union was in complete solidarity with the strikers, told members they could picket off the clock, and told them not to take over striking students' duties.

reason: Acted for prevailing wage.
expectedDescription: Voted to restore Michigan's prevailing wage law, which sets minimum pay rates on state construction jobs. It passed the House 56-53.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted to repeal Michigan's right-to-work law for public employees. The change let unions again charge fees to workers they represent. It passed the House 56-53.

reason: Acted for project labor agreements and prevailing wages.
expectedDescription: Provided public comment to the Nevada Legislature's Regional Rail Transit Advisory Working Group on March 18, 2026, recommending that regional rail development consider project labor agreements or prevailing-wage protections for construction jobs.

reason: Acted against union security contracts.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on third reading of SB 19, the Missouri right-to-work law barring any requirement that a worker join or pay dues to a labor organization as a condition of employment; the House passed the bill 100-59 and the governor approved it on 2017-02-06.

reason: Acted for stronger collective bargaining rights.
expectedDescription: Prime-sponsored SHB 1575, which strengthened collective bargaining rights by governing union membership authorizations and revocations. The bill was enacted into law as Chapter 230, Laws of 2019, with the governor's action recorded on 2019-04-30.

reason: Acted against local minimum wage for state workers.
expectedDescription: Prime-sponsored a law exempting the state from local minimum wage rules for state workers covered by union contracts, and barring cities from taxing the state like a business. The Governor signed it on June 2, 2026 (Senate Bill 26-193).

reason: Acted for opposing a bill against collective bargaining.
expectedDescription: As FOP Lodge 22 secretary and a bargaining representative, Sabrina Tapp-Harper submitted official testimony opposing Maryland HB 1034 as anti-union and harmful to collective bargaining over Baltimore deputy-sheriff wages.

reason: Acted for defending the voter-passed sick time and minimum wage laws.
expectedDescription: As executive director of Mothering Justice and a named plaintiff in the case, publicly condemned the Michigan Court of Appeals ruling that upheld the Legislature's 'adopt-and-amend' gutting of the voter-initiated earned paid sick time and minimum wage laws, calling it a devastating blow to workers.

reason: Acted against public sector union bargaining.
expectedDescription: Jordan D. Teuscher sponsored H.B. 267, Public Sector Labor Union Amendments, which the Governor signed into law.

reason: Acted against unemployment pay for striking workers.
expectedDescription: Cast a recorded floor vote of Nay on ESHB 1893 (unemployment insurance benefits for workers during strikes and lockouts) in the Washington House on 2024-02-12; the roll call was recorded 53-44 in favor.

reason: Acted for faster first union contracts.
expectedDescription: Shri Thanedar signed a discharge petition to force a House vote on the bipartisan Faster Labor Contracts Act, intended to speed first contracts for newly unionized workers.

reason: Acted for raising the minimum wage.
expectedDescription: In a Community Impact candidate Q&A, stated support for raising the minimum wage, improving healthcare access, and reopening rural hospitals.

reason: Acted against public employee bargaining.
expectedDescription: Voted for Wisconsin Act 10, which sharply limited collective bargaining for most state and local public employees.

reason: Acted for bargaining rights for student employees.
expectedDescription: Prime-sponsored SHB 1570 in the Washington House; the governor signed it into law on 2026-03-18 as Chapter 113, Laws of 2026, and the act extended collective bargaining rights to certain employees enrolled in academic programs at public institutions of higher education.

reason: Acted for repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted to let unions again charge fees to non-members in a bargaining unit. That repealed Michigan's right-to-work rule for private employers. The House passed it 56 to 53.

reason: Acted for farm worker labor standards.
expectedDescription: Was identified as a chief sponsor of Oregon HB 2545, a bill establishing agricultural-worker labor standards and protections against termination without cause.

reason: Acted against the tipped wage and sick time laws.
expectedDescription: Joined House Republican colleagues on Dec. 19, 2024 in a public announcement that they were withholding their votes on further bills until House Democrats took up changes to Michigan's tipped-wage and earned sick time laws.

reason: Acted for wage theft penalties.
expectedDescription: Authored Senate Bill 261 on wage theft judgments, which passed the California Senate. It would name delinquent employers publicly and add triple penalties for long-overdue judgments.

reason: Acted for the minimum wage.
expectedDescription: Joint-authored HB 193, relating to the minimum wage; it was referred to the House Workforce subcommittee.

reason: Acted for minimum wage for patient workers.
expectedDescription: The House adopted Walsh's amendment to the 2022 supplemental operating budget requiring Western State Hospital and Eastern State Hospital to pay the state minimum wage to patients working in vocational rehabilitation and work readiness programs.

reason: Acted for paid sick leave and minimum wage.
expectedDescription: Spoke at a Missouri Jobs with Justice rally in support of preserving voter-approved paid sick leave and minimum-wage protections under Proposition A.

reason: Acted for keeping voter-passed minimum wage and sick leave.
expectedDescription: Helped filibuster House Bill 567 in opposition to reversing voter-approved minimum-wage increases and guaranteed paid sick leave under Proposition A.

reason: Acted for workers' compensation for frontline state workers.
expectedDescription: Introduced Nebraska Legislative Bill 444, which bars cities and counties from cancelling the health insurance of a first responder seriously injured in an assault on duty, and brings frontline state employees under the state workers' compensation act. The governor approved it on April 27, 2017.

reason: Acted for equal pay for city contractors.
expectedDescription: Christopher Ward authored San Diego's Equal Pay Ordinance for city contractors, which the City Council advanced in 2017.

reason: Acted for banning noncompete agreements.
expectedDescription: Waxman's House Bill 2558 passed the House to prohibit noncompete agreements for broadcast reporters, anchors, producers, editors and other media workers.

reason: Acted against repealing right-to-work.
expectedDescription: Voted against letting unions again charge fees to non-members in a bargaining unit. That repealed Michigan's right-to-work rule for private employers. The House passed it 56 to 53.

reason: Acted against prevailing wage.
expectedDescription: Voted against bringing back Michigan's prevailing wage law. The law sets union-scale pay on state construction jobs. The House passed it 56 to 53.

reason: Acted for child labor enforcement.
expectedDescription: White was a joint lead sponsor of Ohio House Bill 150, the Clock Out Kids Act, introduced on March 4, 2025. The bill proposes requiring school staff to report certain child labor law violations, raising penalties for those violations, and creating a fund to pay for enforcement.

reason: Acted for raising the minimum wage.
expectedDescription: Led SB 1 as first-named sponsor in the 26th Alaska Legislature, raising the Alaska minimum wage; the bill became law as Chapter 56, Session Laws of Alaska 2009.

reason: Acted against local minimum wages.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on Alabama House passage of HB174. The Alabama Uniform Minimum Wage and Right to Work Act barred local minimum wage ordinances. The measure passed 71-31 on February 16, 2016.

reason: Acted against union security contracts.
expectedDescription: Voted yes on Alabama House passage of HB37, the constitutional amendment writing Alabama's right-to-work policy into the constitution; the measure passed 69-33 on February 17, 2016.

reason: Acted for injured workers choosing their doctor.
expectedDescription: Co-sponsored House File 530 in 2009, proposing to let injured Iowa workers have more say in choosing the doctor who treats them under workers' compensation. The bill was referred to the Labor committee and did not advance.

reason: Acted for paid sick leave.
expectedDescription: Voted for ESSB 5793, paid sick leave; the Senate passed it 28-21.

reason: Acted for charging an employer that skipped workers' compensation insurance.
expectedDescription: As Johnson County Attorney, Rachel Zimmermann Smith filed trial information charging Hawkeye Waste Systems and four officers with failing to maintain workers' compensation insurance after a workplace death.
